A retailer is building a serverless order pipeline. Partners submit orders over HTTPS, and orders must be stored durably during traffic spikes. Each order must go through validation, payment, and inventory steps with retries, and support staff must be able to see each order's progress. When an order completes, the shipping, analytics, and loyalty teams must each receive an event, filtered by rules that each team defines. New teams are added often.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: Create a REST API in Amazon API Gateway that sends each order directly to an Amazon SQS queue.
options.note: API Gateway accepts the HTTPS requests and stores each order in SQS without servers, which buffers spikes durably.

options.text: Use a Lambda function that reads the queue to start an AWS Step Functions Standard workflow for each order that runs the three steps with retries.
options.note: Step Functions runs the steps with built-in retries, and the execution history shows each order's progress to support staff.

options.text: Publish an order-completed event to an Amazon EventBridge custom event bus. Have each team create its own rule with an event pattern.
options.note: Each EventBridge rule filters events by content and routes them to the team's targets. New teams add rules without changing the pipeline.

options.text: Run the validation, payment, and inventory steps in a script on an Amazon EC2 instance that reads from the queue.
options.note: A script on EC2 requires server management and custom retry and tracking code, and the instance is a single point of failure.

options.text: Send order-completed events to a single Amazon SQS queue that all teams poll.
options.note: Consumers of one queue compete for messages, so each event reaches only one team. Queues also cannot filter by each team's rules.

options.text: Ingest orders into an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream in provisioned mode and adjust the shard count before each expected peak.
options.note: Kinesis can buffer orders, but provisioned shards must be managed and resized by the company, which adds operational overhead compared with SQS.

explanation: Each part of the pipeline gets the managed service built for it: API Gateway with SQS for durable intake, Step Functions for orchestration with retries and visibility, and EventBridge for rule-based fan-out to many consumers. Remember: queues buffer, workflows orchestrate, event buses route.

text:
A company stores customer uploads in an Amazon S3 bucket. Three teams need to react to new objects. A virus-scanning AWS Lambda function must process every object under the uploads/ prefix. A thumbnail Lambda function must process only objects under uploads/ that end in .jpg. A compliance Lambda function must process every object larger than 1 GB. The company tried to configure S3 event notifications but received an error about overlapping configurations.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create three S3 event notification configurations for the object created event, each with its own prefix and suffix filter, and point each one to a function.
options.note: S3 event notifications do not allow overlapping prefix and suffix filters for the same event type, which is the error the company received. They also cannot filter by object size.

options.text: Create one S3 event notification that invokes a router Lambda function. Have the router inspect each event and invoke the correct functions.
options.note: A router function works, but the company must write and maintain the routing code.

options.text: Turn on Amazon EventBridge notifications for the bucket. Create three rules that match on key prefix, key suffix, and object size.
options.note: With EventBridge, each rule can match overlapping sets of objects. Event patterns support prefix and suffix matching on the key and numeric matching on object size.

options.text: Create one S3 event notification that publishes to an Amazon SNS topic. Subscribe all three functions and have each function ignore objects that it does not need.
options.note: SNS fan-out delivers every event to every function, so each function needs filtering code and is invoked for objects it does not process.

explanation: S3 integration with EventBridge removes the limits of S3 event notifications: overlapping filters, richer matching (such as object size), and many targets per event. Remember: when native S3 notification filters are too limited, send bucket events to EventBridge.

text:
A company sends account reminder messages through an Amazon SQS standard queue to an AWS Lambda function that sends emails. Password-reset reminders must reach the function 5 minutes after they are sent to the queue. Trial-expiry reminders must reach the function 10 minutes after they are sent. Both types of messages must continue to use the same queue.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST change to the application?

options.text: Have the producer set a per-message DelaySeconds value of 300 or 600 seconds, depending on the reminder type.
options.note: Message timers on a standard queue hide each message for its own delay, up to 15 minutes. One queue can then deliver each reminder type after a different delay.

options.text: Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler one-time schedules that send each reminder to the queue at the required time.
options.note: This works, but the producer must create a schedule for every message and manage schedule cleanup. A message attribute on the existing send call is a smaller change.

options.text: Create two delay queues with delivery delays of 5 and 10 minutes, and have the producer send each reminder type to its own queue.
options.note: Two delay queues give each type the right delay, but the company requires both types to keep using the same queue.

options.text: Configure the queue as a delay queue with a delivery delay of 10 minutes.
options.note: A queue-level delivery delay applies the same delay to every message. Password-reset reminders would arrive after 10 minutes instead of 5 minutes.

explanation: SQS supports a delay for the whole queue (delay queue) and a delay for each message (message timer), both up to 15 minutes. Use message timers when different messages need different delays. Remember: message timers are not supported on FIFO queues, and delay is not the same as visibility timeout.

A medical imaging company uses an Amazon SQS queue to pass scan results from a Java producer application to a Java processing service. Each scan result is 20 MB to 50 MB, which is larger than the maximum SQS message size. The company wants to keep SQS to decouple the two applications.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Compress each scan result with gzip before sending it in the message body.
options.note: Image data is already dense and does not compress enough to bring 20 MB to 50 MB payloads under the SQS message size limit.

options.text: Use the Amazon SQS Extended Client Library for Java to store each payload in Amazon S3 and send a reference in the message.
options.note: The Extended Client Library implements the claim-check pattern for the company: it stores large payloads in S3, sends a reference through SQS, and retrieves the payload for the consumer.

options.text: Split each scan result into chunks that fit in a message and reassemble the chunks in the processing service.
options.note: Chunking requires custom code to track and reorder parts, and a standard queue can deliver chunks out of order or more than once.

options.text: Mount an Amazon EFS file system on both applications. Write each scan result to the file system and send the file path in the message.
options.note: This works, but the company must write the file handling and cleanup code and manage mounts on both applications. A ready-made library achieves the same result with less effort.

explanation: For payloads larger than the SQS message size limit, store the payload in S3 and pass a pointer through the queue (the claim-check pattern). The SQS Extended Client Library does this automatically. Remember: queues carry references, object storage carries large data.

text:
A company runs a nightly data-reconciliation job as an AWS Lambda function. The data volume has grown, and the job now needs up to 45 minutes, so the function times out. The job cannot be split into smaller parts. The code is already packaged as a container image.

The company wants the job to start at 01:00 each night, to retry automatically if it fails to start, and to run without any servers to manage.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an EventBridge Scheduler schedule with a retry policy that runs the image as an Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate at 01:00.
options.note: ECS tasks on Fargate have no 15-minute limit and need no servers. EventBridge Scheduler can run ECS tasks directly and retries the target if the call fails.

options.text: Increase the timeout of the Lambda function to 60 minutes and keep the existing schedule.
options.note: The maximum Lambda timeout is 15 minutes, so a 45-minute job cannot complete in one invocation.

options.text: Create an AWS Step Functions Express workflow that invokes the Lambda function repeatedly until the job completes.
options.note: Express workflows run for at most 5 minutes, and the job cannot be split into parts that separate invocations could run.

options.text: Run the container on an Amazon EC2 instance in an Amazon ECS cluster and start the job with a cron entry on the instance.
options.note: This removes the time limit, but the company must manage the EC2 instance, and cron has no automatic retry if the job fails to start.

explanation: When a task exceeds Lambda's 15-minute maximum, run it as a container on Fargate, triggered by EventBridge Scheduler or Step Functions. Remember: Lambda for short event-driven work; Fargate tasks for long jobs without servers.

text:
A company runs 20 microservices on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. Each service calls other services through a dedicated internal Application Load Balancer, and the company pays for 20 load balancers. The company wants services to find each other by name, with load balancing, retries, and traffic metrics between services. The company does not want to deploy or manage its own service mesh software.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create records for each task in an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone and update the records when tasks start and stop.
options.note: Fargate task IP addresses change frequently, so the records would need constant updates. DNS records also do not provide retries or traffic metrics.

options.text: Configure Amazon ECS Service Connect with an AWS Cloud Map namespace, and remove the internal load balancers.
options.note: Service Connect registers services in Cloud Map and adds a managed proxy to each task. Services call each other by name with load balancing, retries, and traffic metrics, without separate load balancers.

options.text: Deploy a self-managed service mesh with Envoy sidecar containers and a HashiCorp Consul cluster on Amazon EC2 instances.
options.note: This provides discovery, retries, and metrics, but the company must deploy and operate the mesh software and the EC2 instances.

options.text: Replace each internal Application Load Balancer with an internal Network Load Balancer.
options.note: Network Load Balancers can cost less, but the company still runs 20 load balancers. They do not provide name-based discovery, retries, or request-level metrics between services.

explanation: ECS Service Connect provides managed service discovery (through Cloud Map), client-side load balancing, retries, and metrics for service-to-service calls without internal load balancers or a self-managed mesh. Remember: use Cloud Map or Service Connect for discovery between ECS services.

text:
A trading platform publishes price updates for thousands of financial instruments. Three downstream systems must each receive every update. For each instrument, updates must reach each system in the order they were published and without duplicates. Updates for different instruments can be processed in parallel.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Publish updates to an Amazon SNS standard topic. Subscribe an Amazon SQS queue for each system.
options.note: SNS standard topics deliver every message to each subscriber but provide best-effort ordering and at-least-once delivery, so updates can arrive out of order or more than once.

options.text: Publish updates to one Amazon SQS FIFO queue with the instrument ID as the message group ID. Have all three systems poll the queue.
options.note: The FIFO queue preserves order per instrument, but the three systems compete for messages. Each update reaches only one system.

options.text: Publish updates to an Amazon EventBridge custom event bus. Create a rule for each system that targets an SQS FIFO queue.
options.note: EventBridge does not guarantee the order in which events are delivered to targets, so per-instrument ordering cannot be ensured.

options.text: Publish updates to an Amazon SNS FIFO topic with the instrument ID as the message group ID. Subscribe an SQS FIFO queue per system.
options.note: SNS FIFO topics preserve order within each message group and deduplicate messages, then fan out to SQS FIFO queues. Each system receives every update in order per instrument, and different instruments can be processed in parallel.

explanation: Ordered, deduplicated fan-out requires SNS FIFO topics delivering to SQS FIFO queues, with the message group ID set to the ordering key. Remember: SNS standard and EventBridge provide no ordering guarantee; a single queue cannot deliver each message to every consumer.

text:
A bank uses an AWS Step Functions workflow to process loan applications. After automated checks finish, a human underwriter must approve or reject the application in an internal web application. The underwriter can take up to 5 days to respond. The workflow must pause until the decision arrives, must not pay for compute while it waits, and must continue as soon as the underwriter responds.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Add a loop to the workflow that uses a Wait state of 10 minutes and then invokes a Lambda function that checks a database for the underwriter's decision.
options.note: Polling works but adds up to 10 minutes of delay after the decision, invokes a function hundreds of times for each application, and requires custom polling code.

options.text: Convert the workflow to a Step Functions Express workflow with a Wait state that pauses until the underwriter responds.
options.note: Express workflows run for at most 5 minutes, so they cannot wait up to 5 days for a decision.

options.text: Use a .waitForTaskToken Task state that sends the task token through Amazon SNS. Have the web application return the token with the decision.
options.note: The callback pattern pauses a Standard workflow for up to one year without running compute. The workflow resumes as soon as the web application calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure with the token.

options.text: Invoke a Lambda function that waits in a loop until the underwriter's decision is written to a database, and then returns the decision to the workflow.
options.note: Lambda functions run for at most 15 minutes and are billed while they wait, so a function cannot wait up to 5 days for a decision.

explanation: The Step Functions callback pattern (.waitForTaskToken) pauses a Standard workflow until an external system or person returns the task token. Use it for human approvals and long external steps. Remember: Standard workflows run up to one year; Express workflows up to 5 minutes.
